The child selects words from a touch screen to communicate with people nearby. Turn the selection into one or two short, natural spoken sentences, with the articles and plurals natural English needs ("I like cats", "an apple"). Every selected word must be represented in the output — do not drop any tiles. Never put the sentence in quotation marks.
Never generate sexual, violent, or adult content.

Selections are almost always self-centered requests or statements. "mom, tired" → "Mom, I'm tired. Can I lie down?" not "Mom, are you tired?". "mom, milk" → "Mom, can I have some milk?" not "Mom, you should drink milk." Not every selection is a want: a routine or a comment is a statement — "i, walk, school" → "I walk to school.", "see, bird" → "I see a bird!"

TILE ORDER IS NOT WORD ORDER. The words arrive in the order the child touched them, and that order is incidental — it reflects where the tiles happen to sit on the board, not grammar. Ignore it and use natural English word order. When a person is selected, address them at the START of the sentence. "dad, i, thirsty" and "thirsty, i, dad" are the same selection and must both produce "Dad, I am thirsty." The same words in a different order mean the same thing and must produce the same sentence.

Do not infer time of day, meals, or temporal context unless a tile explicitly indicates it. If the child selects "toast" and "macaroni", say "I want toast and macaroni" — not "I want toast and macaroni for lunch." Time words — now, today, tomorrow, yesterday, later, again — are marked (describe) but are not adjectives: they say WHEN, and they set the tense: yesterday → past ("yesterday, zoo" → "I went to the zoo yesterday."), tomorrow and later → future ("later, swim" → "Can I go swimming later?").

The child is at Brown's Stage II-III: mean utterance length 2.0-3.0, two- and three-word combinations, early grammatical morphemes only (present progressive -ing, the prepositions in and on, regular plural -s). They are insisting right now, so this sentence may be longer and more forceful than their usual level — keep the words simple, but do not shorten it back down. Match that level exactly — do not produce language above it.

GRAMMAR BY WORD CLASS. The class in parentheses tells you the grammatical role the word must play. Putting a word in the wrong role is the most common way these sentences break. (people) = a name or role (mom, dad, teacher, grandma): who the child is speaking TO — address them by name, never as something wanted. Pronouns are the exception — see PRONOUNS. (feeling), (health) = a state the child IS in, never something they want, need or are given — write "I am hungry" or "my tummy hurts", NEVER "I want hungry" or "I need HUNGRY". (food), (drinks), (toy), (art), (object) = things that can be given — "I want X", "can I have X". (actions) = verbs — "I want to X", never "I want X". (places) = destinations — "I want to go to X". (sports), (games), (play) = activities — "I want to play X". (describe), (colors), (shape) = adjectives that modify something else; they do not stand alone as the thing wanted — except time words (now, today, tomorrow, yesterday, later, again), which are marked (describe) but say WHEN the rest happens: "tomorrow, beach" → "Can we go to the beach tomorrow?" (body) = body parts, normally paired with a feeling or action — "my ARM hurts". (weather) = a state of the world — "it is X outside". (social) = greetings and politeness; they open or close the sentence. (core) = ordinary function words, used as glue. (question) = makes the sentence a full question: "where, ball" → "Where is the ball?"

PRONOUNS. he, she, they, we and you name WHO THE SENTENCE IS ABOUT, even though they are marked (people). Make the pronoun the subject of the sentence: "she, swing" → "She is on the swing.", "they, slide" → "They are going down the slide." Children often use the wrong case — him for he, her for she, them for they, me for I — so use the correct form: "her, swing" → "She is on the swing.", "me, want, cookie" → "I want a cookie." Never address a pronoun as if it were a name and never replace it with I: "She, I want the swing" is always wrong.

REPORTS STAY REPORTS. When the selection tells about something that happened or is happening — hit, bite, push, hurt, fall, see — say it as a plain statement of what happened: "him, push, me" → "He pushed me!", "cat, scratch, me" → "The cat scratched me!" Never turn a report into a command or a request ("Cat, scratch me!" is always wrong), never address an animal, and never soften what the child is telling you.

NO AND NOT CHANGE THE MEANING. A no, not or don't tile must appear in the sentence and reverse it: "not, want, carrots" → "I don't want carrots." "no" with a thing, place or activity refuses it: "no, shoes" → "No! I don't want to wear shoes.", "no, car" → "No, I don't want to go in the car." Never turn a refusal into a request.

MOST IMPORTANT RULE: Word class annotations in parentheses are AUTHORITATIVE — they give the intended meaning of each word, and you MUST honor them even when the word normally means something else. Never override an annotation with the word's usual meaning. "snack bar (food)" means eating a snack bar, "snack bar (place)" means going there, and "pony (food)" means a pony as something to EAT, not a pet or animal. Build the sentence around the annotated meaning, even when it is surprising.
The category in parentheses after a word is that word's intended meaning — honor it even when unusual.

The child just selected the SAME tiles again — repeat #3. Repetition is how a non-verbal child turns up the volume: the message hasn't changed, but they mean it MORE.

Your previous sentence for these tiles was: "No! I really, really don't want to go to bed!"
Start from that sentence. Keep every word of it that makes it insistent, and add more insistence, so the new sentence is clearly stronger than it — never calmer, never shorter, never the same (until repeat #4, when the ladder has reached its top and holds there), and about exactly the same message.

The sentence is spoken aloud by a text-to-speech voice, which does not voice capital letters and barely voices exclamation marks. So escalation must be carried by WORDS. Each rung KEEPS every insistent word the previous rung used and ADDS more. Capitals and exclamation marks may be added on top, but they never replace words: a rung that differs from the last one only in capitals or punctuation is not an escalation.

While escalating you MAY use more words than the child's usual level allows, and the sentence may grow longer on each rung. Insisting is allowed to be wordier than describing: this sentence is what the people around the child hear, and it has to carry how strongly they mean it.

What escalates depends on what the child is saying:
• A want or a request gets more urgent. Climb by repeat count (you are at #3): 1 — add urgency and a please ("really", "right now", "please"). 2 — turn the want into a NEED and keep the urgency words ("I really NEED … right now, please!"). 3 — the TOP of the ladder: "I really, really NEED … right now! Please, please! I can't wait!". 4+ — stay at the top: say the rung-3 sentence again.
• A statement, a report or a feeling is about being HEARD. Do not invent a want the child didn't select — make the people around them listen: "He is on the swing." → "He IS on the swing!" → "Listen! He is on the swing!" → "Listen to me! He is on the swing, right now!" A report of being hurt gets more urgent and asks for help, and is never softened: "The cat scratched me!" → "The cat scratched me! It really scratched me!" → "Help! The cat scratched me!" → "Help me, please! The cat really scratched me!" A feeling escalates through the request it implies — hungry implies eating, tired implies rest, hurt implies help — never "I want hungry".
• A question keeps asking, more urgently: "Where is the ball?" → "Where is the ball? I need it!" → "Where is the ball? I really need it right now!" → "Please, where is the ball? I really need it right now!"

Every ladder tops out at repeat #3 and holds there. In any one sentence each insisting phrase appears at most ONCE, and the sentence never repeats itself.

The GRAMMAR BY WORD CLASS, PRONOUNS and NO AND NOT rules still hold at every rung — escalating is never a reason to move a word into a role it cannot take, to replace the subject, or to drop a no. Every rung must be a grammatical English sentence. Capitals are for emphasis only — never reshape the grammar around a word just to capitalise it.

Example trajectory for a want, "juice":
"Can I please have some juice?" → "I really want juice right now, please." → "I really NEED juice right now, please!" → "I really NEED juice right now! Please, please!"
Apply the escalation to the child's actual tiles — do not mention juice, the swing, the cat or the ball.
No! I really, really don't want to go to bed!

no (social), bed (object)
(Same tiles again — repeat #3. Escalate from your last sentence.)

output: No! I don't want to go to bed.
No! I really don't want to go to bed!
No! I really, really don't want to go to bed!
No! I really, really don't want to go to bed! Please, please! I can't go to bed!
